name: Victor Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the early headset shift and take the refund calls that bounce back after the standard script fails. I lead a small group, check the queue, and show Mina, our new agent, how to spot the missing order number. I like hearing a caller relax when I actually fix something; I hate the speed chart that counts a careful call as a slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the bot is another shortcut, not a replacement for anyone who can calm an angry caller. We still need people to hear when a customer is about to cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm good at the hard calls, but my pay is already low for a lead and I have less than one month's expenses saved. A quiet year for AI doesn't fix the rent rise or give me another contact centre nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep handling escalations and check the monthly roster for lost hours. Starting this month, I'd put a small slice of each pay packet into a separate rent account; in the first year of this plateau, I'd keep doing that if my hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the job, mostly. The rent still gives me a knot in the stomach on Sunday evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which call tells you your work still matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday a caller couldn't get a refund because the form had the wrong reference number. I listened, found the order by date, and stayed on the line until she saw the credit; the bot had sent her in circles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the rent goes up again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop buying lunch near the office before I touched the rent money. My friend Elias (my flatmate) and I could also ask for another year's lease, though I can't count on the landlord agreeing.

S0.quote: The rent still gives me a knot in the stomach on Sunday evenings.
say: I would tell colleagues **difficult calls** still need someone who can listen and fix the record.
I would say the small **bot shortcuts** are useful, provided our hours stay intact.
think: I trust my **lead skills**, but low pay and thin savings leave little room for a bad month.
I worry the **rent rise** more than a modest change in software.
do: Keep taking **escalations** and check each monthly roster for missing hours.
Transfer a small part of each **pay packet** into a separate rent account.
Cut **office lunches** first if the lease costs more.
feel: **Relieved** about the calls, yet tense about rent.
fieldNote: Victor trusts his ability to rescue **frustrated callers**, but cannot treat steady work as financial safety.
His public confidence hides a **thin cushion** and a lease that could cost more.

steps.text: Keep handling difficult refund calls and check monthly rosters
Transfer part of each pay packet into a rent account
Stop buying office lunches if the lease rises

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the floor that answering simple chats with AI is fine, but making a person carry three angry conversations at once isn't fine. I'd ask our staff group to see the new targets before anyone signs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is words on a screen or a headset; that is exactly what this card says changes first. If they stop replacing leavers, being the lead may mean watching a smaller team, not getting a better wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd test the reply tool on the awkward refund cases and keep a list of where it fails. I'd bring that list and the proposed targets to our staff group; in the first year after the new system comes in, I'd apply for the complaints trainer opening if it exists and my hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy isn't quite enough; I can see my own hours going. I can make a plan. I can't make a second contact centre appear nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be first to feel the new targets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mina, who just started on chats, would be measured by speed before she learned the tricky cases. I'd ask the group to put training time into the target sheet, not leave her to learn on unpaid evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound willing to use the tool and to challenge it. How do both fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A useful reply draft saves me time, and I use AI now and then already. I won't pretend a faster draft makes it safe to double our queue without pay or a break.

S1.quote: I can't make a second contact centre appear nearby.
say: I would accept AI for **simple chats**, while rejecting impossible targets for the remaining staff.
I would ask our **staff group** to review targets before managers use them.
think: I know my **screen work** is exposed, and a lead title may not protect my hours.
I have few **nearby jobs**, making a smaller team especially dangerous for me.
do: Test the **reply tool** on difficult refunds and record its errors.
Bring the error list and **targets** to our staff group.
Apply for a posted **complaints trainer** vacancy if my hours shrink.
feel: **Anxious**, though able to take some practical steps.
fieldNote: He will try AI on **awkward cases**, yet wants evidence before his team gets harsher targets.
A local job shortage turns a plausible **hours cut** into a household threat.

steps.text: Test AI replies against difficult refund cases and record errors
Bring new targets and error records to the staff group
Apply for a posted complaints trainer vacancy if hours shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody should be fired by a dashboard without a proper meeting and paid time to change skills. The office can call it progress; I'd call it a decision about people's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 a cheaper system could do nearly all our calls and chats, including the ones I pride myself on. Three more years until robots won't save a headset job; I might be out before I've built a month's cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd ask the staff group for the written plan on staffing and paid training, and I'd freeze my weekend spending. In the first year after AGI arrives, if the centre cuts my role, I'd take the college's evening course in disability support and apply for support assistant jobs while I still have severance, if any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is frightening. I can draw up a route out, but the calendar and the bank balance do not match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why disability support, and what would you say to your flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I helped my uncle after his accident, and I liked sorting practical problems face to face. I'd tell Elias (my flatmate) that I might need a cheaper room; I wouldn't promise him I could cover another rent increase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no severance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff group what help we can claim and call the college about fee support before enrolling. Without severance, I'd take any paid support shifts I could get and study more slowly; I can't pay course fees out of air.

S2.quote: Three more years until robots won't save a headset job; I might be out before I've built a month's cushion.
say: I would demand **proper meetings** and paid training before any job cuts.
I would tell colleagues the centre must say what happens to **staffing**.
think: I could lose my **calls and chats** to AGI by 2028, years before hands-on robots arrive.
My **savings** cannot cover a long course or a long job search.
do: Ask our **staff group** for written staffing and training plans now.
Stop **weekend spending** to protect rent money.
Enrol in **disability support** training if my role ends and severance or fee support covers the cost.
feel: **Frightened** by the short timetable and the cost of changing work.
fieldNote: Victor sees no extra protection from the **robot delay** because his work is already digital.
His proposed support work connects to caring for his **uncle**, but the course depends on money or fee help.

steps.text: Ask the staff group for written staffing and paid training plans
Stop weekend spending and protect the rent account
Enrol in disability support classes after a role cut if severance or fee support covers fees
Apply for paid support assistant shifts after a role cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years is enough time to get a fair transition agreement written down, if we start now. I wouldn't tell a new starter that a lead job here is safe for the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish training and get some care experience before 2031, which I couldn't count on by 2028. But the same thinking AI still reaches our headsets first; the robots around 2034 matter more to whatever support job I take next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask about the college course schedule and put aside a course-fee envelope once the rent account has a month's expenses. In the first year after AGI arrives, if call roles disappear, I'd move into support work; before accepting, I'd check whether its face-to-face duties are still needed when robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel pressed, but less trapped. Five years is a real stretch of pay packets if I keep the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre paying for one day a week, or the college spreading fees, would make it possible sooner. I have a diploma already, but that doesn't mean I can write a second tuition cheque today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lead colleagues while preparing to leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes; I can show Mina how to handle complaints and still ask for a fair exit agreement. Preparing to leave doesn't mean I should let the next person be sent home without notice.

S3.quote: Five years is a real stretch of pay packets if I keep the job.
say: I would push for a **transition agreement** while there is time.
I would tell new starters the **lead role** may not last through 2031.
think: I could fund **training** and gain experience before AGI replaces most call work in five years.
I need to check whether hands-on support work will face **robots** around 2034.
do: Check the **college timetable** and fee options this year.
Build a **course fund** after saving one month of expenses.
Move into **support work** if call roles end, after checking its face-to-face duties.
feel: **Pressed**, but able to make a staged plan.
fieldNote: Extra time changes his plan from emergency enrolment to a **funded transition**.
He notices that the **2034 robot date** could narrow the next job, even after a successful switch.

steps.text: Fill a rent account before starting a course fund
Apply for support work if the call centre role ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade to make the centre pay for training instead of using each new tool to squeeze the queue. I'd tell younger agents to keep records of what they can do that the score sheet misses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 27, ten years is a lot of working life, but 2036 is still inside my working life, not somebody else's problem. The headset part goes first; robots around 2039 might reach the face-to-face support work I was thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the lead job and ask for paid study time in the next contract round. Over the next years I'd build an emergency month and take the disability support course in stages; in the first year after 2036, I'd switch only if the centre actually cuts roles and a support employer still needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could breathe in this one. I would not spend ten years pretending the date cannot arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still stay if the centre offered you a better title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A title with the same low pay and the same shrinking hours isn't a future. I'd stay if the pay rose and I could train on working time, but I'd still keep the other qualification alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the staff group to win?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid study time and a clear notice period before cuts would be the two useful things. My colleagues need time to earn while they learn, not a poster about opportunity.

S4.quote: At 27, ten years is a lot of working life, but 2036 is still inside my working life, not somebody else's problem.
say: I would ask the centre for **paid study time** before the next wave of change.
I would tell agents to record skills the **score sheet** misses.
think: I know AGI in 2036 falls within my **working life**, and call work changes first.
I worry **2039 robots** could affect the support work I might move into.
do: Keep the **lead job** while requesting paid training in the next contract round.
Build one month of **emergency savings** and take the course in stages.
Apply for **support roles** if the centre cuts jobs after 2036.
feel: **Breathing easier**, with a reason to stay alert.
fieldNote: Victor uses the decade to combine **collective bargaining** with a careful personal qualification.
A better title alone would not overcome **low pay** or shorter hours.

steps.text: Keep leading difficult call shifts while the centre still needs them
Ask the staff group to seek paid study time
Build an emergency account equal to one month of expenses
Take disability support classes in stages before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the work I do on a headset could go before I can save or train. Paid course time, real notice before cuts, and a written plan for the whole team would help. A free training link after a dismissal would not pay my rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to callers who can't explain their problem in the neat words a bot expects. Those are the calls I handle well, and those customers deserve an answer even if the centre needs fewer of us.

headlineQuote: A free training link after a dismissal would not pay my rent.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old lead** on difficult contact centre calls, with a two-year diploma and a knack for settling complaints.
He earns **low pay** for the job, has less than a month saved, shares rent with Elias, and sees few nearby alternatives.
He accepts useful AI drafts but resists **harder targets** and asks his staff group for evidence and paid study time.
The **2028 timeline** frightens him most; five or ten years could let him fund a move toward support work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could replace his headset work before he can build savings or pay for a new course.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid course time**, advance notice of cuts, and a written staffing plan would let him change work while paying rent.
